Caption of first 5:00

Hey guys Elyot here from Lunarch Studios, and today i'm gonna make a quick video about some of our plans for growth and future plans for Prismata. The reason I'm making this video is actually a user on [Redacted] who posted that he noticed that in the Prismata game client, the number of users that it says are online, it used to be a lot higher; now it seems a bit lower. How come? and so I wanted to explain why that number is a little bit lower, and a few things we're going to be doing with growth and new features. One comment is that actually that stat for the current number of online users: that stat has been wrong for a while. 1 it used to count users playing our online demo and were not actually logged in, and 2 that certain crashed users were online for an eternity. If a specific bug happened, that user would never get removed from the system, so we'd restart the server and the number of users would slowly climb, and then we'd reset and it would slowly climb again. The number now is more accurate than it used to be. We have all of our internal stats, and looking at those we can see more details about our actual user activity. During December and January (during and right after the kickstarter), there was a lot more activity on Prismata for sure. It peaked right as kickstarter ended. Only a small number of users who enter the pipe play for the long term. We hit about 500 users a day, 1000 a week. Now we have tools to boost that number (such as sending out keys), but we have to give out dozen's and dozens of keys to get that one long-term user. That said, our numbers are really good considering that we're not open to the public. We have a very small number of key giveaways.

Prismata has no retention features of any kind. There's no daily quest, no stuff you unlock, no email reminders; we don't do any of that stuff. We don't have any of those types of features. We're still seeing steady numbers of players logging into the system. This is actually really good, because it means that those users are playing Prismata because they fundamentally enjoy the game and they want to keep playing, and not because we're pushing them along. Of course, we're going to add a whole bunch of retention features, because they're really important to our growth. The alpha isn't really about growth; it's about testing new features, balancing the units, to see how they affect our current player base, and how to optimize them for performance and to make things work.

December was different; it was when we ran our kickstarter, and we we're doing growth full throttle. We hired a PR firm, I was doing video content every day, doing [Redacted] content every day, all kinds of stuff to really drive growth to help out our kickstarter. I gotta say, I got absolutely nothing done during December that wasn't related to promotion. Kickstarter was a full-time job. We don't want to be doing growth perpetually, as we want to work on our game.

Right now, during the alpha period, what we're mostly focusing on is building up the game, and building up those features that will allow us to grow in the future. Once that's all ready and optimized and really well tailored to our user base, then we can go full throttle with the growth.

Let me talk a bit about some of the barriers to growth that we have to overcome before we start going full throttle. Number one by far is the barrier to entry for new players.

I am 100% a machine embroidery maker, I digitize my own designs and stitch them out, adjust them if needed and then stitch on a final product which is usually leather. I enjoy the journey of creating things, even failures, because I try to learn from everything I do.

I'm starting to move into heat transfers and 3d printing and meshing everything together to make some final products that I like to sell online to support my habit. Which is making more things in unique ways.

Hey there. I'm just getting into Machine Embroidery myself. (First piece i successfully made, without breaking needles or jamming up the machine) http://i.imgur.com/9MIXb9r.jpg

Is there a cheat sheet of sorts? meaning.. types of needles to use on what type of material with what types of thread? Once i get the basics down, I would like to start expanding my horizons. I'm making the above piece into a patch, but looking into appliques for different projects. I'm a totaly Noob at all this.

Busted 3 needles and jammed up the machine 3 times before i realized i was using all purpose (or quilting, not sure which) thread. I'm also really interested in digitizing my own work, cant absolutely cannot shell out hundreds of $$ for the software. Are there any reasonable options, aside from famring out each image to digitizers for 50 bucks a pop or more?

Looks like you are using a canvas or thicker material to stitch into. Have to play with the needle sizes and the tension if you can adjust them manually. I buy larger/oversized eye ballpoint titanium coated needles and use them to stitch into just about everything, I don't switch to sharps for cloth or the blades for leather because I have never seen a real difference. I have some double oversized eye needles that I use for metallic and decorative threads, when I use these I slow my machine down to 400spm and I can put them into anything.

If you are going to stitch this out again I'd suggest getting some proper sized needles if you haven't already, loosen the tension up a good amount and slow your machine down for this thicker stuff. You'd probably see a lot better results around the circles where it gets thin for 10-20 stitches.

Software wise I've never used any of the free programs but there are some better ones that come to mind SophieSew would be one I'd try first, the page looks to have some positive reviews on its use.

For the most part it just takes practice, when I initially started a couple years ago the stuff I'd produce was pretty terrible. I'm always learning but if I set out to do a project 90% of the time now I get it right the first time and I still always do a test stitch before I cut into something valuable; that's just smart money. But also with the most cautious approaches had to get out my stitch ripper and take something out that donked up and ruined the whole design/final product. It happens.

I just got done finally watching the extended Lords of Waterdeep, which is a surprisingly satisfactory way to spend two and a half hours, and I'm feeling particularly well-disposed toward TableTop today.

Seasons 1 and 2 were on point. A few mistakes here and there but nothing too major and they'd usually caught them by the time it aired and added a little editor's note to the video.

Season 3, as has been well documented recently, is a bit of a mess. In about 50% of the games they've made some massive rules errors that don't necessarily make the games less fun or detract from the whole purpose of the Tabletop show but don't really do the games justice.

They obviously spread themselves too thin and dropped the ball on some key things in a very major way. In one of the recent episodes one of the graphics that popped up on screen to show the current scores of the players was totally fucked up with names and photos being mixed up. It's only on screen for a few seconds and not a big deal but the fact that nobody at any stage of the editing process paused it and pointed out that the graphic was totally screwed up is pretty telling as to their production standards in general this time around.

I don't think it would be as big of a deal if they hadn't crowdfunded the season AND dropped the ball.
I find it weird that Wil's version of an apology is blaming someone else for half his post.
It's exactly what I would have expected from him in terms of an apology.

My opinion? Wil and the folks working on Tabletop are still doing an amazing thing. Attracting tons of people to a youtube channel all about board games. Do they get everything right? No. Did they screw up a number of times? Sure. But they're still having a great time playing the game and are doing one of the most important jobs in our hobby.

They are showing how much fun a group of friends can have sitting around a table pushing cards and bits about. That is the biggest, most important thing about this hobby. It's fun, it's interesting and it's worth doing because of those things. If it felt like a job, none of us would do it much.

But what Wil and crew are doing is work - they're putting hours and hours into it and it still looks fun. So sure, there were rules mistakes and yes Wil's unhappy about it and said so very publicly. And he did so in a way that was reactionary, inflamed and very much in the moment. Well, that clinches it. Wil's a human and makes mistakes and stuff. I'll be he goes to the bathroom too and sometimes enjoys eating too much chocolate. That stuff happens and we'll all get over it.

I still enjoy tabletop and I'll continue to watch it because it's fun. If I want to see exactly how to play a game, I'll hunt down a how to play video. If I want to see some interesting people playing, and get a good feel for how a game works, I'll get that from Tabletop.

I kind of appreciate Wil in that he's very "one of us". He reads comments, he participates in the discussions online, he has emotional reactions to things and sometimes posts before really thinking about how he might feel a week later.

You can be damn sure there isn't a PR manager sitting in the wings supervising his internet activity because he puts his foot in his mouth and gets involved in silly internet troll shenanigans almost constantly. I've been subsribed to his Facebook feed for about 6 months now and at least once a month I'll see something there and just think "Dude, what the fuck are you doing? Stop feeding the trolls!"
